You aren't just passing the necessary data, you're forcing the receiving system to spin up massive amounts of computational overhead just to read a simple string of text. We're basically forcing the agent to carry the metadata of every single tool in his active working memory at all times. Which is why Yin et al. recognized that this was a deeply inefficient bundling of features. And so they designed an alternative, which is the at-skills protocol. Right. So let's look at Yin's solution before diving into the deep math that explains why it works. The at-skills protocol is essentially this exercise in aggressive unbundling. Highly aggressive. Yin and their team looked at the install paradigm. They looked at the positional attention bottleneck. And they decided to shatter the installation process into three distinct isolated tiers. And these are based on what actually incurs a token cost and what genuinely triggers reliably in an LLM. Exactly. Let's walk through those piers, starting with Tier 1, the bare reference. This is the foundation of the whole unbundling thing. In Tier 1, there is no installation step at all. You simply type a path like at Giddy Veserbolskil directly into your chat message to the agent. So what is happening architecturally under the hood when a user does that? Okay. So when the agent's orchestration layer encounters that bare reference, it halts the standard inference cycle. It just stops. Then it resolves that network path, fetches the raw markdown content of the skill, and injects it exactly at the point of execution within that specific message turn. So it's basically just-in-time dependency resolution. Essentially a JIT dependency resolution, yes. But here is the critical architectural distinction. Once that specific inference turn is complete, the context window collapses back to its baseline state. Oh, wow. Yeah. The fetched skill is garbage collected. It leaves absolutely no standing memory footprint in the ongoing system prompt. So the standing token cost for having that skill available for your next request is zero. Zero tokens. That's incredible. You bypass the prompt limitation entirely because you only pay the token cost precisely at the millisecond you are actively invoking the tool. Exactly. But Yin's team also recognized that pulling from a remote repository on every single turn isn't always practical. I mean, you have network latency, versioning instability, maybe offline development environments. Right. You can't always rely on an external ping. Exactly. So that brings us to tier two, the saved copy. In this tier, the skill is vendored into your project's local Git-tracked file tree. Okay. So this is a localized dependency. You're pulling the skill.md file down to your local hard drive. But again, where is this file indexed? It is indexed entirely by your external non-LLM tooling. Ah, okay. It sits on disk, it's tracked by Git, it's integrated into your IDE, but it remains completely outside the model's context window. The agent has no passive awareness of it. So if you want to use it, you still have to reference its local path. Yes. Therefore, the standing token cost to the prompt remains zero. The prompt is perfectly protected from the sheer volume of your saved skills. Which brings us to the final piece of the puzzle, tier three, the installed line. This is the only mechanism in the entire AdSkills protocol that touches the system prompt. And you only invoke tier three when you're purchasing one very specific property, right? Yes. The ability for the agent to auto-trigger the skill without the user explicitly naming the path. That's right. When you promote a skill to tier three, the protocol generates a dot auto-trigger entry. This takes a highly condensed piece of front matter, basically a description of what the skill does and when to use it, and permanently pins it into the resident system prompt. And what does that cost? It costs anywhere from 50 to 100 precious tokens per skill. So Yin's team empirically proved that simply reading a skill's content does not actually require that skill to be resident in the prompt. They effectively decoupled the concept of availability from the concept of residency. You only pay the 50 token prompt tax when you explicitly require the auto-triggering behavior. Exactly. But this is exactly where the fliction paper steps in. And honestly, this is where I initially had some serious pushback. Oh, really? What was your hesitation? Okay, here's where it gets really interesting, because this is where we transition from software engineering into pure type theory, and we aren't going to water this down. Fliction anchors this entire argument in John Reynolds' 1983 theory of relational parametricity, and specifically Philip Wadler's famous 1989 paper, Theorems for Free. Yes, Wadler's paper is legendary in functional programming. So we need to unpack what a free theorem actually is in the context of polymorphic functions. Let's do it. So in functional programming, a polymorphic function is one that is defined uniformly over a generic type variable. It's designed to operate on a container, like a list, a tree, or a stream, without needing to know anything about the specific data types residing inside that container. Right. So a list of integers, a list of strings, a list of complex objects, the polymorphic function interacts with the structure of the container, not the semantics of the elements. Okay, and Wadler asked a highly specific question about these functions. If you apply an arbitrary transformation to the underlying data within the container, does the polymorphic function operating on that container still behave identically? Exactly. Does its internal logic transport across the transformation automatically, simply by virtue of its type signature? Or do you have to establish an explicit binding rule, a hypothesis, to guarantee that the function won't break? Right. And Wadler proved that these functions basically bifurcate into two fundamental categories. The first category consists of what he called genuinely parametric functions. These are unconditional. Functions like head, which extracts the first element of a list, or tail, which returns the list minus the first element, or frist, which projects the first element of a tuple. Right. So if I have a generic list a, and I apply an arbitrary function f to transform every element of a, Wadler's theorem dictates that extracting the head of the list first and then transforming that single extracted item yields the exact same result as transforming the entire list first and then extracting the head. The operation commutes flawlessly. Flawlessly and unconditionally. The head function doesn't care if the data changes from integers to strings, or if it moves from one memory register to another. Because its specification is completely silent on the properties of the data, it demands no structural assumptions from that data. You get the preservation of its behavior entirely for free. I always think of the head function like this. It's like saying, it doesn't matter if I pull the top card off a deck and then paint it blue, or if I paint the whole deck blue and then pull off the top card, the result is the identical blue card. No special rules needed. That's exactly right. But then Wadler identifies the second category, conditional functions. And this includes operations like sort, filter, and fold. Right. Heavy hitters. Yeah. And these functions cannot be genuinely parametric because they are forced to consume additional structure to execute their logic. Okay, let's break down the sort example because this is crucial. Right. So look closely at sort. You cannot sort a generic container without an ordering relation. The function fundamentally relies on the ability to compare element X to element Y and determine precedence. Therefore, if you apply an arbitrary transformation F to your data, does sort commute? No, absolutely not. Like, if I have an ordered list of integers and my transformation F is a cryptographic hash function, the resulting hashes will not preserve the numerical order of the original integers. The data is scrambled, and the sort operation's output is corrupted because the assumed structure was destroyed. Precisely. Therefore, sort does not yield a theorem for free. Commutation for sort requires an explicit binding hypothesis. You can only apply a transformation if that transformation strictly preserves the ordering relation. The structure must be protected. Exactly. You are mathematically obligated to purchase that protection if you want the function to survive the change. Wait, hold on. If that token cost in the at-skills protocol is actually the physical artifact of this structural obligation, then prompt engineering isn't just about hacking the system with clever keywords. It is literally applied type theory. We are negotiating mathematical boundaries using token economics. Yes. Flixion says, let's look at the three tiers of Yin's protocol resolve, save, and trigger, and map them directly onto Wadler's functional categories. Okay, let's do that. In this mapping, the transformation we are applying isn't changing an integer to a string. It's a change in representation. It is the act of moving a skill from a remote server to a local disk to an active memory cache. We are changing where and how the data physically lives. Let's trace that execution path. Flixion maps this to Flixion's tuple projection function. Let's dig into the memory pointer mechanics of this because this is where the architecture really shines. It's very clever. When you save a skill locally in the AdSkills protocol, you aren't just downloading raw text. You are actually generating a tuple composed of two elements, the content itself and a provenance stamp. The provenance stamp is vital metadata. It records the exact origin URI, the commit hash, the timestamp, and the localized dependency graph. It is the audit trail. But when the agent's runtime environment calls the resolve function on that locally saved skill, the architecture deliberately executes a projection. It takes the tuple of content and provenance, isolates the content, and injects only the content into the LLM's context window. The provenance stamp is left entirely behind on the disk. It aggressively drops the second half of the tuple, exactly like Flixion. And by doing so, it creates a non-interference guarantee. You can update the provenance stamp. You can change the local file path. You can alter the git commit history. You can apply vast representational transformations to the metadata. But because the runtime structurally ignores everything but the content during injection, the execution remains perfectly invariant. Another free theorem. Zero standing token cost. But then we hit tier 3. Auto-triggering. The trigger operation. Flixion maps this directly to sort. And this is where the free theorems end. Completely end. Because trigger consumes additional structure. To allow an agent to passively monitor a user's prompt and spontaneously decide to invoke a tool, the agent must have continuous resident awareness of that tool's capabilities. Right. It can't trigger what it doesn't know exists. Exactly. The operation is not defined over bare, floating data. It is fundamentally defined over a resident prompt. Residency is the ordering relation of the LLM architecture. If you apply a representational transformation that removes the skill's front matter from the acts of context window, say, migrating the skill back to a purely local disk file does trigger commute. It breaks instantly. The agent becomes completely blind to the skill. It will never auto-trigger a tool it cannot see in its attention matrix. Exactly. Therefore, the trigger operation carries a strict, inescapable hypothesis. Any change in the system must preserve the prompt residency of the skill. And this is Flixion's breakthrough insight. This part blew my mind. That 50 to 100 token cost for the auto-trigger front matter. That isn't sloppy coding by Yin's team. It isn't an arbitrary tax. It is the physical computational materialization of the explicit hypothesis that the sort function mathematically requires. If you want the conditional feature of auto-triggering, you are mathematically forced to pay for the structural assumption that makes it possible. Yin et al. didn't invent this boundary. But Flixion pushes this further, because once you understand the strict residency requirements of trigger, you have to ask, how do these requirements scale when we attempt to execute complex, multi-step workflows? Right. Let's say I'm building an autonomous agent to handle a complex code refactor. I needed to use a repository search skill to find the relevant files, a static analysis skill to identify the bugs, and a get-commit skill to push the fixes. In the traditional install paradigm, where everything relies on auto-triggering, I have to rely on what Yin calls the trigger lottery. The trigger lottery is the direct result of probabilistic matching in a resident prompt. If you dump all three of those skills into the active context window, the LLM has to independently evaluate the semantic relevance of each skill's front matter against your prompt. It has to guess. Right. It has to probabilistically guess, ah, I need the serve skill, and then independently it has to guess, I also need the static analysis skill. And since it's an LLM, every independent evaluation is subject to stochastic variation. If you have a 90% chance of successfully auto-triggering each skill, your chance of flawlessly triggering all three in the correct sequence drops to about 72%. If you need five skills, you're essentially flipping coins. The architecture guarantees a decay in reliability as complexity increases. But Wadler proved that fold requires an exceptionally strong hypothesis to survive transformation. It requires an algebra homomorphism condition. The transformation must strictly preserve the specific combining operation itself. How does that mathematical condition map to executing our multi-step code refactor? The first is what Fliction labels Fliction, which stands for semantic obligations. Right. A semantic obligation is the bedrock requirement for an operation to retain its fundamental identity. It's what must be preserved for an operation to remain itself. For our resolve operation, the act of fetching and reading a file, the Fliction is strictly bound to content identity. Every operation, regardless of its design, carries an inescapable power one dollar. But then we introduce the second invariant, a PRE, which stands for representational obligations. This is the supplemental structural luggage that a specific implementation or feature set demands in order to execute successfully. This is the hypothesis we were talking about earlier, like reading a skill via a bare reference has an empty PREA. It demands zero extra structure. But auto-triggering a skill has a massive, complex power end. It demands either strict prompt residency or perfect index synchronization across a distributed database. The bundling pathology. Yeah. This pathology infects a system when an architect takes multiple operations, some with an empty PREA and some with a massive power, and irreversibly fuses them together behind a single, opaque user interface. Like the ubiquitous install button. Exactly. When you bundle operations this way, you trigger what Fliction terms commitment leakage. The massive representational obligations of the auto-trigger feature bleed out and contaminate the simple read feature. And the pointer-level mechanism of this leakage is insidious. Because the system only exposes the bundle, the execution runtime is forced to allocate the memory, track the state, and maintain the structural hypotheses for all sub-operations. Even if the user only intends to utilize the simplest one. So the operation's individual luggage is smaller than the bundle's luggage, but the system forces you to carry the entire bundle anyway. It's economically disastrous at scale. The pathology becomes fatal because the system inherently prices the entire interface at the rate of the most expensive internal operation. You are forced to pay the 50-token prompt tax, the heavy prep of the trigger operation, for a skill that you only ever needed to resolve once. It is a systemic design defect. It is not an unavoidable physical reality of artificial intelligence. It's a human failure to respect mathematical boundaries in software architecture. A well-designed system charges an operation only for its specific representational structure. So what does this all mean? Well, by unbundling the interface, Yin et al. cured the pathology. They physically severed the memory pointers connecting the resolve execution path from the trigger state requirements. They allowed you to execute operations with an empty prep without paying the toll for the heavy prep features. Flyxion beautifully terms this cured state commitment honesty. A commitment honest system is one where the architectural cost of an operation is strictly proportional to its inherent representational obligations and absolutely nothing else. It refuses to charge you for the structural assumptions of features you aren't invoking. Commitment honesty. I want to highlight that phrase because it is an incredibly powerful lens through which to view not just AI but all software engineering. This paper proves that forcing operations with no representational commitment to pay the cost of operations that do have them is a design defect, not a physical necessity of AI. The primary goal was never to build a perfect truth machine. The goal was not to build a commercial product that guarantees a flawless essay every single time you hit enter. The goal was to build a research architecture where failures are localizable. Where we can finally see exactly where the machine broke down. Yes. When a monolithic black box AI chat interface produces a bad essay, you learn absolutely nothing about artificial intelligence. You just get a bad essay. Right. But when this pipeline produces a bad essay, when it homogenizes a novel idea, or when the revisor stubbornly ignores the reviewer, you can open the files and find out exactly where and why it failed. You can see the exact line where the reviewer flagged the novel idea as an error. You can see the exact moment the revisor enacted that erasure. By making the failure visible and material, we can actually study and improve AI cognition. So it's a diagnostic tool for researchers. Exactly. We can test different prompt structures. We can measure empirically if swapping the 8B model for a 12B model fixes the homogenization problem. The pipeline is an experimental apparatus designed to help us understand AI, not just a tool to churn out text. So what does this all mean, bringing all of this together for the listener? It means a lot. What Fliction's 2026 paper is really showing us is that the future of artificial intelligence might not be what we see in sci-fi movies or tech keynotes. Definitely not. It might not be a single opaque, omniscient superbrain sitting in a server farm that we just blindly trust with our prompts. The evidence strongly suggests that the future of productive, reliable, safe AI is likely compositional. Compositional. It is a transparent, modular, highly constrained assembly line where we can inspect every single thought process, every logical plan, and every critique as a saved text file on a local hard drive. It is entirely about breaking the illusion of the magic generation button and taking physical, architectural control over the trajectory of machine thought. And in doing so, we fundamentally demystify the technology. We stop treating these language models as infallible digital oracles and start treating them as what they actually are. A sequence of bounded, fallible, probabilistic operations that absolutely require strict human oversight and rigid architectural constraints to produce truly reliable work. Which leaves me with one final, deeply provocative thought that I want to leave you, the listener, with today. Oh, let's hear it. Building heavily on what we've learned about this pipeline architecture. If forcing an AI to externalize its memory into physical files, if forcing an AI to logically plan its dependencies before it is allowed to speak, if forcing an AI to endure isolated negative cognitive friction makes it so much more effective and logically sound, shouldn't we be building this exact same strict pipeline for human thought? That is a fascinating application of the pipeline theory to human psychology. Imagine a future digital workspace where you, the human employee, are physically not allowed by your software to send a project proposal or an email. Until what? Until a local system forces you to stop, step out of your flow state, and write out your unstated assumptions into an inspectable review.md file. What if the ultimate hidden value of this entire AI architecture isn't just that it teaches us how to deconstruct and debug machine generation? What if it serves as a mirror? Exactly. What if it teaches us how to deconstruct, inspect, and debug our own flawed, impulsive, black box human reasoning? It forces us to confront the reality that human cognition is often the original black box. Yes. Because whether you are a biological human or a massive language model running on a GPU, sometimes you just need to stop, step back, look at the raw ingredients sitting in the separate bowls on your kitchen island. And here is the terrifying punchline of the paper. However, conventional economics cannot tell these two societies apart. Their GDP is identical. Their average standard of living is identical. Consumer satisfaction surveys might even be identical. But Society A has accumulated durable competence. Society B has only accumulated fragile artifacts. Society B is brittle. If a massive disruption occurs, a political collapse, a geomagnetic storm that wipes out data centers, a shift in corporate incentives, or an economic catastrophe, the artifacts will remain for a while, just like the Roman aqueducts. But the capacity to regenerate those systems, to fix them when they break, will rapidly vanish. So what does this all mean? Well, when you strip away all the academic terminology, the hashing algorithms, a history of calculus, the core warning of this source material is that we are currently making a silent, unacknowledged trade. We are trading our permanent civilizational memory for temporary capability. We are trading the messy, slow, occasionally frustrating, but incredibly resilient process of distributing knowledge for the frictionless, lightning-fast, incredibly fragile process of renting convenience. What's fascinating here is how this framework redefines the entire purpose of technology. The author concludes that the highest purpose of technological innovation isn't actually making sophisticated machines. It's not. The machines, the software, the AI, they're just a byproduct. The true purpose of technology is expanding humanity's representational repertoire. Representational repertoire. Explain that. They fundamentally expanded humanity's shared capacity to think. Oh, I see. That geometry and that physics became a permanent part of who we are as a species. They gave future generations a richer conceptual foundation to stand on. That is true progress. When a tool becomes a new language for human thought, civilization advances. When a tool just performs a magic trick behind a proprietary curtain, we really consume. And that puts the responsibility squarely on us, on the consumers, and crucially on the engineers and institutions building the next generation of infrastructure. Because the AI models, the cloud platforms, the digital ecosystems, they don't have an intrinsic bias toward opacity. They can be built as ladders or they can be built as walls. They can be engineered to transfer competence, to act as educators, or they can be built to hoard it, to act as oracles. It is an architectural choice. It is entirely a choice. The technology itself cannot determine which future emerges. It depends on whether our economic structures continue to exclusively reward the artificial scarcity of competence, or whether we demand systems that leave behind more capable human minds after every interaction. A civilization only truly remembers its inventions when its citizens remember how to invent. Which brings us all back to you, listening to this right now. So the social contract is a promise about the future. And when Mars vanishes, the contract is totally void. The institution is instantly, fundamentally bankrupt. If there is no destination, why should anyone obey the navigator? The captain's power, his entire mandate to rule, is derived exclusively from his ability to steer the ship to safety. If steering is physically impossible, his authority loses its entire justification. The leaders delay the truth not just to protect the passengers from despair, but to protect their own legitimacy. The author notes that authority will often exert massive energy to preserve a representation of reality that the physical environment no longer supports, just to avoid giving up power. You see this in the real world constantly. Think about a massive corporation that is secretly going bankrupt. The CEO knows the math doesn't work. The technical truth is that the company is dead, but they don't tell the lower-level employees. Middle management is still demanding quarterly reports, still doing performance reviews, still enforcing dress codes, all while the ship is sinking. Exactly. The illusion of normalcy. They enforce the theater of a future to extract the last bits of present labor. It's incredibly cynical, but mathematically logical from the perspective of the power structure. It is the exact same dynamic. The captain of the Anyara has to pretend to navigate just to keep people from realizing navigation is a dead concept. But as the monograph points out, epistemic delay has an expiration date. You can't hide it forever. No. Eventually, the truth bleeds out. Rumors spread from the engineering decks. Which brings us to the sociological phenomena the author calls the inward turn. When the macro goal, the grand project of arriving at Mars, completely disappears, the micro goals violently inflate to fill the vacuum. Because you still need a reason to get out of bed in the morning, even if the bed is floating in the abyss. Exactly. You have this massive contraction of the reachability field. The horizon shrinks from millions of miles to the few hundred yards of the ship's interior. It becomes claustrophobic. And the author points out that this spatial and temporal collapse causes a total radical redistribution of scarcity. Before the accident, physical resources and currency mattered because they could be converted into a better future on Mars. You save your credits to buy a bigger plot of land when you land. Makes sense. But when no one can buy a ticket home, when landing is impossible, material wealth loses its convertibility. It becomes functionally meaningless. You can have all the digital credits in the ship's mainframe, but you're still stuck in the exact same metal tube, breathing the exact same recycled air, eating the exact same paste as the poorest person on board. Now, I look at that setup, and my instinct is to think, doesn't a disaster like this act as the ultimate social equalizer? You're all literally in the same boat. If money doesn't matter, and the future is canceled, doesn't hierarchy just naturally collapse into a sort of egalitarian survival commune? It's a very logical, perhaps hopeful assumption, but the text explicitly and forcefully counters this. Catastrophe does not abolish stratification. It merely mutates what stratification can buy. Oh, wow. The author argues that social distinctions actually become hyper-important precisely because environmental novelty has dropped to absolute zero. Outside the hull of the ship is an unchanging, infinite, lethal void. Inside the ship is a highly constrained, repetitive, unchanging architecture. Everything is gray metal and fluorescent light. Just totally sterile. So where do people find variation? Where do they find status when they can't buy property? They find it in each other. The social drama becomes the only landscape left. Yes. Scarcity migrates. It migrates away from material wealth and attaches itself to intangible things. Access to restricted information, an extra square meter of private space, psychological relief, intimacy, and most importantly, proximity to power. Like who knows the captain? Right. Being allowed into the command center or becoming a high priest in one of the bizarre new cults that form on the ship, that becomes the new currency. The society starts producing internally the chaotic variation that the external environment no longer supplies. People become utterly vicious over microscopic social slights because that social standing is the only reality they have left. There's a specific image from the text that I absolutely love, and it perfectly encapsulates this inward turn. It's the metaphor of the mirror at the window. Oh, that part is so evocative. The author writes that normally when you look out the window of a moving vehicle like a train or a car, you see changing landscapes. Trees go by, mountains appear, cities rise and fall. The window gives you constant information from the external environment, and it confirms that you are making progress. Right. It proves you're moving. But in deep space, looking out the window just gives you an unchanging, pitch-black void. The stars are so far away, they don't even appear to move. So eventually, after months of staring into the black, you stop trying to look out the window. You shift your focus entirely to the reflection on the glass, and you only see yourself and the interior of the cabin. It is a stunningly bleak and perfectly accurate metaphor for what the author calls epistemic closure. Because there is no external feedback that matters anymore, no changing landscape to respond to, no new data entering the system, society literally folds inward and starts feeding on itself. Just a closed loop. Exactly. Institutions begin to only observe other institutions. A ritual is performed simply to validate another ritual.
